adjudication_records.issue_text: Any error during the Salesforce token refresh (rate limit, revoked token, missing app keys) throws HttpError 400 in the SalesforceCalendarService constructor, killing operations that previously succeeded with the still-valid cached access token — a cascade from transient upstream conditions to total Salesforce breakage

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the constructor now unconditionally performs a refresh-token fetch to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and throws `HttpError` when `response.statusText !== "OK"` (e.g., rate limits, revoked token, missing/invalid keys). There is no fallback path to proceed using the existing `credential.key` access token when refresh fails, so a transient refresh failure will prevent creating the `jsforce.Connection` and break operations that could have continued with the cached token.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The response.statusText !== 'OK' check in the Salesforce refresh is fragile because undici returns an empty statusText for HTTP/2 responses, turning successful refreshes into spurious 400 errors

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the new refresh flow rejects based on `if (response.statusText !== "OK")` and throws a 400. Using `statusText` for success/failure is fragile (it can vary by runtime/transport and may be empty), so a successful HTTP 200 response could be misclassified as an error. A robust check would use `response.ok` or `response.status`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: zoho-bigin passes credentialId instead of credential.userId as the calcomUserId argument to refreshOAuthTokens (zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:91), so the sync endpoint looks up the wrong entity (or none) and returns wrong or absent tokens for the user

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the call to `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes `credentialId` as the third argument. The helper `refreshOAuthTokens` is defined to take `userId: number | null` and, when syncing is enabled, posts `calcomUserId: userId.toString()` to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. Other integrations in the diff consistently pass `credential.userId`. Passing a `credentialId` (credential record id) instead of the Cal.com user id would cause the sync endpoint to look up the wrong user.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The webhook secret is compared with a plain !== string comparison (non-constant-time), which is timing-attack-vulnerable for a secret guarding an endpoint that can overwrite any user's app credentials; a constant-time compare such as crypto.timingSafeEqual should be used

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added endpoint `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the webhook secret is validated via a direct `!==` comparison: `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. This is not a constant-time comparison and can be vulnerable to timing attacks against a secret that gates an endpoint capable of creating/updating credentials for arbitrary `userId`s. Using `crypto.timingSafeEqual` (with proper Buffer normalization) would mitigate this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The webhook's findFirst → create sequence has a TOCTOU race: two concurrent calls for the same user+app can both miss in findFirst and both create, leaving duplicate credentials because there is no unique constraint on userId+appId

adjudication.rationale: In the new webhook handler `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the code does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and then conditionally `credential.create(...)` if none is found. That check-then-act pattern is a classic TOCTOU race: two concurrent requests for the same `(userId, appId)` can both observe no row and both attempt to create. If there is no DB-level unique constraint on `(userId, appId)` this can create duplicates; even if there is, one request will fail with a unique-violation error because the sequence is not atomic. The diff itself shows the non-atomic pattern and even notes “Can't use prisma upsert…”, implying lack of a suitable unique key.

adjudication_records.issue_text: findFirst in the webhook has no deterministic ordering when multiple credential rows already exist, so updates target an arbitrary row

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler uses `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId: reqBody.userId, appId: appMetadata.slug } })` without an `orderBy`. If multiple matching credential rows can exist, Prisma will return an arbitrary match and the subsequent `credential.update({ where: { id: appCredential.id } })` would update a non-deterministic row. The diff does not show whether `(userId, appId)` is uniquely constrained in the schema, so the defect only manifests if duplicates exist.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The webhook handler has unhandled throw paths that produce 500s instead of 4xx responses: there is no req.method check (a GET hits zod .parse(undefined)), and malformed bodies, wrong encryption keys, or non-JSON plaintext in symmetricDecrypt/JSON.parse all throw unhandled

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler does not check `req.method` before calling `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)`. For non-POST requests (e.g., GET), `req.body` may be `undefined`/empty, causing `zod.parse` to throw a `ZodError`, which is not caught and would surface as a 500. Additionally, `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` and the subsequent `JSON.parse(...)` are not wrapped in try/catch; wrong/missing encryption keys or non-JSON decrypted plaintext will throw and likewise produce unhandled 500s instead of a controlled 4xx response.
